*Numbers source:* every value in this document is transcribed from
`v2/report/v2_report_numbers_collected.json`, which records the WORK output
file each number came from. Nothing here is computed in prose; the three
derived percentages are computed in that JSON with their formulas recorded.

## What this run is and why it exists

The v1 concept mapper classified roughly 7,000 questions from 47 Census
Bureau demographic surveys into a shared topic and subtopic taxonomy, then
coded harmonization barriers for candidate question pairs between source
surveys (CPS, FoodAPS) and the ACS. Those findings were produced by one
generation of models. If they cannot be reproduced by a different
generation, they are an artifact of a particular model rather than a
property of the surveys.

The v2 confirmation run reruns the pipeline over the same 6,987 questions
with a new ensemble: `claude_4_5_sonnet` and `gemini-2.5-flash` as
independent raters, arbitrated by `claude_4_5_opus`, all routed through the
USAi harness. AHS was added as a net-new survey with no v1 baseline. Prompt
equivalence between generations is gated by the TEVV prompt-equivalence
check: 21 divergences between v1 and v2 prompts, every one acknowledged and
justified, gate exit 0. Directional-bias hypotheses attached to those
divergences are *provisional* pending SME review and are not findings of
this report.

## Headline findings

1. Topic-level classification reproduces across model generations. Final
   adjudicated agreement is 92.0 percent (kappa 0.880). Cross-generation
   raw-rater agreement (91.25 percent, best pair) exceeds v1's own
   within-generation rater agreement (89.24 percent), so the v1-to-v2 gap is
   no wider than the noise floor inside v1 itself.
2. Subtopic-level agreement is materially lower (76.9 percent final, kappa
   0.761) and the confusion structure is the same in both generations:
   Social versus Economic at topic level, the Expenditures, Expenses, and
   Purchases cluster at subtopic level. The taxonomy boundary, not the model
   generation, is the binding constraint.
3. Disagreement concentrates where v1 was already uncertain. Questions v1
   resolved by rater agreement reproduce at 97.5 percent topic agreement;
   questions from v1's arbitrated, new-concept, and unresolved strata fall
   to 85, 66, and 16 percent respectively.
4. The Stage 3 discard floor reproduces. Of v1's F3 discards on the common
   pair set, 96.7 percent (CPS) and 97.4 percent (FoodAPS) are discarded
   again by v2.
5. The candidate set partially turns over, in the strict direction. v2
   retains 68 percent of v1 candidates; demotions to F3 outnumber promotions
   roughly four to one (46 versus 11 CPS, 27 versus 8 FoodAPS). The
   direction is consistent with the documented F3-attractor, which remains
   prompt-confounded and unresolved.
6. The dual-generation gold set is 62 candidate pairs (40 CPS, 22 FoodAPS):
   pairs both generations independently rated harmonizable at high
   confidence. This is the defensible bridge-variable lead list.
7. AHS, net-new in v2: of 736 unique AHS questions that entered pairing
   against ACS, 89 (12.1 percent) have at least one candidate match, 47
   best-tier F1 and 42 best-tier F2. 259 of the 736 share no subtopic with
   ACS at all and are genuinely AHS-specific territory. Question counts are
   unique question texts; an id-based version of these figures (92 of 744)
   was retired as inflated. The AHS candidates carry single-generation
   provenance and are unvalidated leads, not results.

## Stage 1: independent rater agreement (n = 6,987 questions)

The first question is whether individual raters from different generations
even see the questions the same way, before any adjudication smooths the
answer. The table compares every rater pairing: within v2, within v1, and
across generations.

| comparison | topic % | topic kappa | subtopic % | subtopic kappa |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v2a vs v2b (within v2) | 90.64 | 0.859 | 71.38 | 0.704 |
| v1claude vs v1openai (within v1) | 89.24 | 0.839 | 69.69 | 0.687 |
| v1claude vs v2a (cross) | 91.25 | 0.868 | 76.23 | 0.753 |
| v1claude vs v2b (cross) | 89.55 | 0.844 | 67.74 | 0.667 |
| v1openai vs v2a (cross) | 89.72 | 0.845 | 71.52 | 0.706 |
| v1openai vs v2b (cross) | 89.83 | 0.848 | 71.18 | 0.703 |

The cross-generation rows sit inside the same band as the within-generation
rows. A v2 rater agrees with a v1 rater about as often as two v1 raters
agree with each other, which is the operational definition of
interchangeable raters. The subtopic ceiling near 70 to 76 percent appears
in every pairing regardless of generation, which locates the limit in the
taxonomy's subtopic boundaries rather than in any model.

## Stage 2: final adjudicated classification, v1 vs v2 (n = 6,987)

After arbitration resolves rater disagreements, each generation produces
one final classification per question. This compares those finals head to
head.

| metric | value |
|---|---|
| topic agreement | 92.03% (kappa 0.880) |
| subtopic agreement | 76.90% (kappa 0.761) |
| full (topic + subtopic) agreement | 76.00% |
| v1 unresolvable | 0 |
| v2 unresolvable | 10 |

Reproduction stratified by how v1 reached its answer:

| v1 decision method | n | topic agreement % |
|---|---|---|
| agreement | 4,765 | 97.5 |
| auto_dual_modal | 821 | 85.1 |
| pick_gpt5mini | 522 | 84.7 |
| pick_haiku45 | 482 | 83.4 |
| new_concept | 340 | 66.5 |
| dual_modal | 19 | 52.6 |
| unresolved_disagreement | 31 | 16.1 |
| categorization_failed | 7 | 14.3 |

The gradient is monotone in v1's own certainty: the easier a question was
for v1's raters, the more faithfully v2 reproduces it. Classification
instability is not random noise added by the new generation; it maps the
questions the taxonomy never cleanly held. For the 68 percent of the
corpus that v1 resolved by simple rater agreement, the v1 classifications
can be treated as generation-stable.

## Stage 3: harmonization barrier reproduction (CPS, FoodAPS vs ACS)

### Pair universe intersection

Stage 3 operates on question pairs, and which pairs exist depends on the
upstream subtopic assignments. Because subtopics shifted on roughly a
quarter of questions, the v1 and v2 pair sets themselves only partially
intersect. Every agreement number below is conditioned on the common pairs
and is silent about the rest.

| survey | v1 pairs | v2 pairs | common | Jaccard |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CPS | 603 | 659 | 480 | 0.614 |
| FoodAPS | 459 | 667 | 390 | 0.530 |

### Agreement on common pairs

| survey | n | L1 barrier % (kappa) | feasibility % (kappa) | both % |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CPS | 480 | 84.8 (0.518) | 83.5 (0.604) | 74.6 |
| FoodAPS | 390 | 92.6 (0.674) | 88.5 (0.652) | 83.6 |
| combined | 870 | 88.3 (0.576) | 85.8 (0.625) | 78.6 |

Raw agreement and kappa diverge because the class distribution is dominated
by the CC barrier and the F3 tier, which inflates agreement-by-chance. Both
numbers are reported and neither alone is the result.

### Candidate dynamics on common pairs

The deliverable unit of Stage 3 is the candidate set: pairs rated F1
(direct recode) or F2 (statistical adjustment). This table tracks what
happened to v1's candidates under v2.

| metric | CPS | FoodAPS |
|---|---|---|
| v1 candidates (F1/F2) | 144 | 86 |
| v2 candidates | 109 | 67 |
| intersection | 98 | 59 |
| demoted (v1 candidate, v2 F3) | 46 | 27 |
| added (v2 candidate, v1 F3) | 11 | 8 |
| binary candidate agreement | 88.1% (kappa 0.696) | 91.0% (kappa 0.717) |
| both-discard reproduction | 96.7% | 97.4% |
| gold set (dual-generation, high confidence) | 40 | 22 |

Two asymmetries matter. First, discards are far more stable than
candidates: when v1 said a pair was not harmonizable, v2 almost always
agreed, so the negative finding is the most reproducible result in the
study. Second, v2 is systematically the stricter rater, removing about a
third of v1's candidates while adding few of its own. Whether that
strictness reflects better judgment or an artifact of the acknowledged
prompt divergences is exactly the question the TEVV directional-bias review
(open, SME pending) exists to answer; this report does not prejudge it.
The practical consequence either way: the 62-pair gold set, which requires
agreement from both generations, is robust to the question.

## AHS: net-new coverage (no v1 baseline)

| metric | value |
|---|---|
| unique AHS questions entering pairing vs ACS | 736 |
| questions with at least one candidate (F1/F2) | 89 (12.1%) |
| best tier F1 / F2 | 47 / 42 |
| entered pairing, all pairs F3 | 388 |
| no shared subtopic with ACS | 259 |
| candidate pairs / total pairs | 130 / 1,626 (8.0%) |
| F3 pair share | 92.0% |

Question counts are unique question texts, the project's certified unit; 4
texts carrying duplicate ids previously inflated these figures to 92 of
744, and the id-based numbers are retired to a diagnostics block.

Reach is heavily structured by topic. Demographic questions reach 64.3
percent because AHS asks the same age, race, sex, and relationship
questions ACS does; Housing, the bulk of the survey at 360 questions
producing pairs, reaches 11.1 percent because AHS's housing content goes
far deeper than ACS's. The 259 no-shared-subtopic questions are the
cleanest finding: genuinely AHS-specific content with no ACS counterpart
territory, which is the enrichment case for AHS in one number. Full
subtopic tables, candidate listings, and the unvalidated-floor caveat are
in `output/stage3/results/ahs/ahs_rollup.md` (WORK).

## Limitations

The Stage 3 agreement numbers are conditioned on the common-pair
intersection; roughly 40 percent of each generation's pair universe has no
counterpart in the other and is not assessed. AHS candidates are
single-generation and unvalidated. The kappa values for Stage 3 reflect
heavy class imbalance and should be read alongside raw agreement, not
instead of it. The v2-stricter pattern is confounded with acknowledged
prompt divergences until the TEVV directional-bias review closes. Ten
questions v2 marked unresolvable had v1 classifications; they are counted
as disagreements, not dropped.

## Bottom line

The v1 findings survive the generation change where it matters. Topic
classifications are generation-stable, discards reproduce at 97 percent,
and the candidate signal concentrates into a 62-pair dual-generation gold
set that no single model produced alone. The instability that does exist
is informative rather than damaging: it sits on taxonomy boundaries and on
questions v1 itself could not resolve, and v2's stricter candidate
judgment narrows the lead list rather than contradicting it.
